Definition: Essential processes (nutrition, respiration, transport, excretion) that must occur continuously to maintain living organisms
Process of taking in food and converting it into energy and body materials; autotrophic (self-made) or heterotrophic (from outside)
Mode of nutrition where organisms synthesise their own food from inorganic sources using light energy (photosynthesis) or chemical energy
Mode of nutrition where organisms obtain food by consuming other organisms; includes herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
Process by which green plants convert CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen using sunlight energy trapped by chlorophyll
Green photosynthetic pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue) for photosynthesis
Organelles in plant cells containing chlorophyll; site of photosynthesis; found mainly in mesophyll cells of leaves
Pores in leaf epidermis surrounded by guard cells; allow CO₂ entry and O₂ exit during photosynthesis; also permit transpiration
Cells flanking stomata that regulate their opening (turgid) and closing (flaccid); control gas exchange and water loss
Biological catalysts (proteins) that speed up chemical reactions in the body without being consumed; e.g., amylase, pepsin, trypsin
Enzyme in saliva that breaks down starch into simpler sugars (maltose); begins carbohydrate digestion in the mouth
Wave-like muscular contractions of alimentary canal walls that push food along the digestive tract from mouth to anus
Muscular tube connecting mouth/pharynx to stomach; food moves through it by peristalsis; also called food pipe/gullet
Muscular J-shaped organ where food is churned and mixed with gastric juice (HCl, pepsin, mucus); begins protein digestion
Glands in stomach wall that secrete gastric juice containing HCl, pepsin and mucus
Protein-digesting enzyme secreted by stomach as inactive pepsinogen; activated by HCl; works in acidic conditions
HCl secreted by stomach; activates pepsinogen to pepsin; kills bacteria in food; creates acidic pH (~2) for digestion
Slimy secretion lining stomach wall; protects stomach from self-digestion by pepsin and HCl
Ring of muscle controlling passage between digestive organs; e.g., pyloric sphincter between stomach and small intestine
Longest part of alimentary canal (~7 m); main site of digestion and absorption; receives bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice
Largest gland in body; secretes bile stored in gall bladder; involved in metabolism, detoxification and production of bile salts
Alkaline digestive secretion made in liver, stored in gall bladder, released into small intestine; emulsifies fats; no digestive enzymes
Salts in bile that emulsify large fat droplets into smaller ones (emulsification) increasing surface area for lipase action
Mixed gland near duodenum; endocrine (secretes insulin/glucagon) and exocrine (secretes pancreatic juice with trypsin, lipase, amylase)
Secretion of pancreas containing trypsin (digests proteins), lipase (digests fats) and amylase (digests carbohydrates); released into duodenum
Protein-digesting enzyme in pancreatic juice; works in alkaline conditions in the small intestine
Fat-digesting enzyme in pancreatic juice; breaks down emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Finger-like projections on inner wall of small intestine; increase surface area for absorption; contain blood capillaries and lacteals
Part of alimentary canal after small intestine; absorbs water and minerals from undigested food; forms faeces
Process of breaking down food (glucose) to release energy (ATP); occurs in all living cells; aerobic or anaerobic
Respiration using oxygen; glucose → CO₂ + water + ATP; releases more energy (36–38 ATP per glucose); occurs in mitochondria
Respiration without oxygen; glucose → pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂ (in yeast) or lactic acid (in muscle cells); releases less energy (2 ATP)
3-carbon compound produced from glucose during glycolysis; entry point for aerobic (→ Krebs cycle) or anaerobic (→ lactate/ethanol) pathways
Adenosine triphosphate; energy currency of the cell; produced during cellular respiration; provides energy for all cellular activities
Anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast or bacteria; glucose → ethanol + CO₂; used in bread-making and brewing
Product of anaerobic respiration in animal muscle cells under oxygen deficiency; causes muscle fatigue and cramps
Tiny air sacs in lungs; very thin walls (one cell thick); rich blood supply; site of gas exchange (O₂ into blood, CO₂ out)
Dome-shaped muscular sheet below lungs; contracts (flattens) during inhalation to increase chest volume; relaxes during exhalation
Iron-containing protein in red blood cells; binds O₂ in lungs (oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it to tissues; also carries CO₂
Muscular organ with four chambers (2 atria + 2 ventricles); pumps blood through pulmonary and systemic circuits; ensures double circulation
Upper left chamber of heart; receives oxygenated blood from lungs via pulmonary veins
Upper right chamber of heart; receives deoxygenated blood from body via vena cava
Lower left chamber of heart; pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body through aorta; thick muscular walls
Lower right chamber of heart; pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs via pulmonary artery for oxygenation
Blood vessels carrying blood away from heart; thick elastic walls; carry oxygenated blood (except pulmonary artery)
Blood vessels carrying blood toward heart; thin walls with valves to prevent backflow; carry deoxygenated blood (except pulmonary vein)
Microscopic blood vessels with single-cell-thick walls; connect arteries to veins; site of exchange between blood and tissues
Cell fragments in blood; initiate blood clotting; release clotting factors at wound sites
Colourless fluid similar to plasma; collects interstitial fluid; carried by lymph vessels; transports fats from intestine (lacteals)
Loss of water vapour from plant surfaces mainly through stomata; creates negative pressure (transpiration pull) drawing water up xylem
Suction force created by water loss from leaves that pulls water upward through xylem from roots; primary mechanism for water ascent
Vascular tissue conducting water and dissolved minerals from roots to all parts of plant; dead cells with lignified walls
Vascular tissue transporting dissolved food (sucrose) from leaves to all parts including roots; active, energy-requiring process
Transport of food (dissolved sugars) through phloem from source (leaves) to sink (roots, growing parts, storage organs)
Pressure generated by osmotic absorption of water from soil into roots; pushes water up xylem; important in young plants
Removal of metabolic waste products (urea, CO₂, excess water/salts) from the body to maintain homeostasis
Structural and functional unit of the kidney; consists of Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, proximal/distal tubules and loop of Henle
Pair of bean-shaped excretory organs; filter blood to form urine; regulate water and salt balance; maintain blood composition
Tube carrying urine from kidney to urinary bladder
Main nitrogenous waste in humans; formed in liver from breakdown of excess amino acids; excreted in urine by kidneys
Cup-shaped structure at the beginning of nephron surrounding the glomerulus; filtrate from blood enters here during ultrafiltration
Medical procedure filtering waste from blood using an artificial kidney when kidneys fail; blood passes over a semi-permeable membrane
Circulatory pattern in which blood passes through heart twice per circuit — pulmonary (heart→lungs→heart) and systemic (heart→body→heart)
Force exerted by blood on vessel walls; measured with a sphygmomanometer; normal ~120/80 mmHg (systolic/diastolic)
Blood pressure when heart ventricles contract and push blood into arteries; higher value (~120 mmHg); measured with sphygmomanometer
Blood pressure when heart ventricles relax and refill; lower value (~80 mmHg); blood pressure never falls to zero
Condition of persistently elevated blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg; risk factor for heart disease and stroke
Instrument used to measure blood pressure; readings give systolic and diastolic pressure values
System of nerve cells and tissues that regulates and coordinates body functions by electrical impulses; includes CNS and peripheral NS
Structural and functional unit of nervous system; consists of cell body (with nucleus), dendrites and axon; can be up to 1 metre long
Short branched extensions of neuron cell body; receive signals from other neurons and sensory receptors
Long single extension of neuron; transmits nerve impulses away from cell body toward synapse with another neuron or effector
Junction between two neurons or between neuron and effector; impulse crosses via neurotransmitter chemicals released from axon terminal
Sensory cells or organs that detect stimuli (light, sound, touch, chemicals); convert stimuli into electrical signals sent to nervous system
Taste receptor cells on tongue that detect chemical stimuli; send signals to brain via sensory neurons
Smell receptor cells in nasal epithelium; detect airborne chemicals; send signals to brain for smell perception
Involuntary, rapid automatic response to a stimulus that does not require conscious brain involvement; e.g., knee jerk, withdrawal from heat
Neural pathway for a reflex action: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector
Part of CNS enclosed in vertebral column; conducts impulses between brain and body; mediates reflex actions
Main coordinating centre of nervous system; divided into fore-brain (thinking/senses), mid-brain and hind-brain (basic functions)
Largest brain region including cerebrum; responsible for thinking, intelligence, memory, voluntary actions and processing sensory information
Brain region between fore-brain and hind-brain; involved in visual and auditory reflexes; involuntary actions
Includes cerebellum (balance/coordination) and medulla (basic involuntary functions like heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure)
Part of hind-brain; coordinates muscle movements, maintains balance and posture; receives sensory information from muscles and joints
Part of hind-brain (brain stem); controls involuntary actions — heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, vomiting, salivation
CNS; comprises brain and spinal cord; processes information and coordinates responses
PNS; all nerves outside brain and spinal cord; includes cranial nerves (12 pairs) and spinal nerves (31 pairs)
Action performed under conscious control of cerebrum; e.g., picking up a pen, walking; involves higher brain centres
Action not under conscious control; regulated by medulla or spinal cord; e.g., heartbeat, breathing, peristalsis
Signal travelling along a neuron as a change in electrical charge across the membrane; propagated by ion movements
Chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands into the bloodstream; regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction and homeostasis
Ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream; e.g., pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads
Plant hormone promoting cell elongation; responsible for phototropism; synthesised at shoot tip; moves away from light
Plant hormones promoting stem elongation, seed germination and fruit development; applied commercially to increase fruit size
Plant hormones promoting cell division; delay ageing (senescence) of leaves; work with auxins to regulate growth
Plant growth inhibitor; promotes stomata closure during drought; induces dormancy in seeds and buds; "stress hormone"
Fight or flight hormone secreted by adrenal glands; increases heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose; prepares body for emergency
Gland above each kidney; adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline; adrenal cortex secretes corticosteroids
Hormone secreted by thyroid gland; regulates metabolic rate, growth and development; requires iodine for synthesis
Butterfly-shaped gland in neck; secretes thyroxin; requires dietary iodine; deficiency causes goitre
Enlargement of thyroid gland due to iodine deficiency; thyroxin cannot be synthesised without iodine
Hormone secreted by beta cells of pancreatic islets of Langerhans; lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake by cells
Male sex hormone secreted by testes; responsible for development of male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty
Female sex hormone secreted by ovaries; responsible for development of female secondary sexual characteristics at puberty
Hormone secreted by pituitary gland; stimulates body growth and cell reproduction; deficiency causes dwarfism
Master endocrine gland at base of brain; secretes hormones that regulate other glands (TSH, FSH, LH) and growth hormone
Period of sexual maturation; triggered by hormones (testosterone in males, oestrogen in females); physical and reproductive changes occur
Condition of high blood glucose due to insufficient insulin production or insulin resistance; treated with insulin injections or diet
Directional growth of plant toward (positive) or away from (negative) light; caused by unequal auxin distribution in shoot
Directional growth response of plants to gravity; roots grow downward (+ve geotropism), shoots grow upward (-ve geotropism)
Directional growth of plant roots toward water; roots bend toward region of higher moisture
Directional growth of plant in response to chemical stimuli; e.g., pollen tube growth toward ovule guided by chemicals
Plant movements in response to directional stimuli (light, gravity, water, chemicals); caused by differential growth
Regulatory system where the output of a process inhibits further output; maintains hormone levels within normal range (homeostasis)
Biological process by which organisms produce offspring; ensures continuation of species; does not maintain individual life but preserves species
Replication of DNA before cell division; accuracy is vital but occasional errors introduce variation; fundamental to inheritance
Differences among individuals of a species; introduced by errors in DNA copying during reproduction; raw material for evolution
Asexual reproduction by splitting; binary fission (into two equal cells) in bacteria and Amoeba; multiple fission in Plasmodium
Asexual reproduction where a cell divides into two equal daughter cells; e.g., Amoeba, Leishmania, bacteria
Asexual reproduction where nucleus divides multiple times then cytoplasm divides; produces many daughter cells; e.g., Plasmodium (malaria parasite)
Asexual reproduction where an organism breaks into fragments, each developing into a new individual; e.g., Spirogyra
Ability of an organism to regrow lost parts or regenerate a whole organism from a fragment; e.g., Hydra, Planaria
Asexual reproduction where a bud forms as an outgrowth, grows and eventually separates; e.g., Hydra, yeast
Asexual reproduction in plants from vegetative parts (stem, root, leaf); methods include cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture
Asexual reproduction by producing spores in sporangia; spores germinate under favourable conditions; e.g., Rhizopus (bread mould)
Spore-producing structures at tips of aerial hyphae of fungi like Rhizopus; release spores when mature
Common bread mould; reproduces asexually by spore formation in sporangia; also shows sexual reproduction
Reproduction involving a single parent; no gametes; offspring are genetically identical to parent; faster but less variation
Reproduction involving fusion of two gametes (male + female); introduces genetic variation; seen in plants and animals
Cell division that produces four haploid gametes from one diploid cell; reduces chromosome number by half
Haploid reproductive cells (sperm and ovum); formed by meiosis; fuse during fertilisation to restore diploid number
Male gametophyte of flowering plants; produced in anthers; contains male gametes; transferred to stigma during pollination
Female reproductive unit inside ovary; contains egg cell; develops into seed after fertilisation
Diploid cell formed by fusion of sperm and egg; first cell of new organism; develops by mitosis into embryo
Early developmental stage from zygote; in plants, enclosed in seed; in animals, early stage before organ differentiation
Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower or same plant; no genetic variation introduced
Transfer of pollen from anther of one plant to stigma of another plant; introduces genetic variation
Sprouting of seed into seedling; requires water, warmth and oxygen; embryo resumes growth
Growing plants from small pieces of tissue (explants) in sterile nutrient medium; produces clones; used for disease-free plants
Mass of undifferentiated cells formed when plant tissue is grown in culture medium; can be induced to form shoots and roots
Age of sexual maturity; males: ~13–14 years; females: ~10–12 years; involves physical changes triggered by sex hormones
Male primary reproductive organs; produce sperm (in seminiferous tubules) and testosterone; located in scrotum
Pouch of skin outside abdomen containing testes; maintains temperature ~2–3°C below body temperature for sperm viability
Duct carrying sperm from testes (via epididymis) to urethra; passes over the bladder
Common duct for semen and urine in males; carries sperm out of body during ejaculation
Male gamete; has head (nucleus/DNA), middle piece (mitochondria for energy) and tail (flagellum for motility)
Glands secreting fructose-rich fluid providing energy and medium for sperm; contribute to semen volume
Gland below bladder secreting alkaline fluid that activates sperm; makes up part of semen
Female primary reproductive organs; produce eggs (one per cycle) and hormones (oestrogen, progesterone)
Oviduct; muscular tube connecting ovary to uterus; site of fertilisation; cilia sweep egg toward uterus
Muscular pear-shaped organ; site of implantation and foetal development; endometrium lining shed during menstruation
Lower narrow neck of uterus opening into vagina; dilates during childbirth
Birth canal connecting uterus to exterior; receives sperm during intercourse; passage for birth and menstrual flow
Monthly shedding of uterine lining (endometrium) and blood when fertilisation does not occur; marks start of new menstrual cycle
Disc-shaped structure attaching foetus to uterine wall; exchanges oxygen, nutrients and wastes between mother and foetus; secretes hormones
Developing human offspring from 8 weeks post-fertilisation to birth; all major organs formed; nourished by placenta
Methods to prevent pregnancy; barrier (condom, diaphragm), chemical/hormonal (pills), intrauterine (Copper-T), surgical (vasectomy/tubectomy)
Barrier contraceptive (sheath) worn on penis; prevents sperm reaching egg; also reduces transmission of STDs
Intrauterine device (IUD) inserted into uterus; prevents implantation of fertilised egg; effective long-term contraceptive
Sexually transmitted diseases including gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV-AIDS; spread through sexual contact; condoms reduce risk
Human immunodeficiency virus causing AIDS; destroys immune cells (CD4 T-cells); transmitted through sexual contact, blood, needles
Illegal termination of female foetuses after prenatal sex determination; causes skewed sex ratio; prohibited in India under PNDT Act
Transmission of traits (characteristics) from parents to offspring through genes; studied by Gregor Johann Mendel using pea plants
Differences among offspring and between offspring and parents; caused by DNA errors in reproduction and sexual reproduction
Passing of genetic information (genes/traits) from one generation to the next through sexual or asexual reproduction
Observable characteristics or features of an organism determined by genes; e.g., height, flower colour, seed shape in peas
Trait that is expressed even when only one copy of the allele is present; represented by capital letter; e.g., tall (T) in peas
Trait expressed only when both copies of the allele are recessive (homozygous); represented by lowercase letter; e.g., dwarf (t) in peas
Gregor Johann Mendel; Austrian monk and scientist; "Father of Genetics"; conducted experiments on pea plants (Pisum sativum) 1856–1863
First filial generation; offspring obtained by crossing two pure-breeding parents (P generation); all offspring show dominant trait
Second filial generation; obtained by self-pollination of F1; shows 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes in monohybrid cross
Segment of DNA coding for a specific protein; unit of heredity; located on chromosomes; each gene has two alleles (in diploid organisms)
Alternative forms of a gene at the same locus on homologous chromosomes; e.g., T (tall) and t (dwarf) are alleles of height gene
Thread-like structures of DNA and protein in nucleus; humans have 46 (23 pairs); carry genes; each parent contributes one of each pair
Chromosomes that determine biological sex; females have XX (two X chromosomes); males have XY (one X and one Y)
Larger sex chromosome; females have two copies (XX); males have one (XY); carries many genes besides sex-determining ones
Smaller sex chromosome present only in males (XY); carries SRY gene that determines male sex; contributed by father to sons
Process by which biological sex is determined; in humans, female egg always contributes X; father's sperm contributes either X (daughter) or Y (son)
Homozygous tall genotype (both alleles dominant); pure-breeding tall pea plant; produces only tall offspring when self-pollinated
Homozygous short/dwarf genotype (both alleles recessive); pure-breeding dwarf pea plant; always shows dwarf phenotype
Heterozygous tall genotype; one dominant (T) and one recessive (t) allele; shows tall phenotype due to dominance of T
Pisum sativum; Mendel's experimental organism; chosen for clear contrasting traits, short generation time and ease of self/cross pollination
Cross between parents differing in two traits; produces 9:3:3:1 ratio in F2 generation; demonstrates independent assortment
Mendel's second law; alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation; genes on different chromosomes
Functional unit of nature; includes all living organisms (biotic) and their physical environment (abiotic) interacting together in an area
Living parts of an ecosystem: producers (plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi)
Non-living parts of an ecosystem: temperature, water, soil, light, air, minerals; determine what organisms can survive
Autotrophic organisms that produce food by photosynthesis; base of all food chains; e.g., green plants, phytoplankton, algae
Organisms that obtain energy by consuming other organisms; classified as primary (herbivores), secondary (carnivores) and tertiary consumers
Organisms that break down dead organic matter into simple inorganic substances; e.g., bacteria, fungi; recycle nutrients in ecosystem
Primary consumers that eat only plants; first animals in a food chain; e.g., grasshopper, rabbit, deer
Consumers that eat other animals; secondary or tertiary consumers; e.g., frog, snake, hawk
Consumers that eat both plants and animals; e.g., humans, crows, bears
Linear sequence of organisms where each feeds on the previous one; e.g., grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle
Interconnected network of multiple food chains in an ecosystem; more realistic representation of feeding relationships
Feeding positions in a food chain; producers are at level 1, primary consumers level 2, secondary consumers level 3, etc.
Only 10% of energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next level; rest is lost as heat during metabolic processes
Transfer of energy through trophic levels; unidirectional (one-way); decreases at each level due to heat loss; unlike nutrient cycling
Progressive increase in concentration of harmful chemicals (e.g., pesticides, DDT) at successive trophic levels; top consumers most affected
Chemicals used to kill agricultural pests; enter food chains and accumulate through biological magnification; e.g., DDT in water bodies
O₃; triatomic oxygen molecule; in stratosphere it absorbs harmful UV radiation protecting living organisms from DNA damage
Shield of ozone (O₃) in the stratosphere (15–35 km); absorbs most UV-B and UV-C radiation; being depleted by CFCs
Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun; causes skin cancer, cataracts and damage to DNA; blocked by stratospheric ozone layer
Thinning of the ozone layer due to CFCs and other chemicals; results in increased UV radiation reaching Earth's surface
Chlorofluorocarbons; used in refrigerants, aerosols and fire extinguishers; react with ozone in stratosphere destroying the ozone layer
United Nations Environment Programme; international body dealing with environmental issues; coordinated the Montreal Protocol on ozone
Materials that can be broken down by decomposers (bacteria, fungi) into harmless substances; e.g., vegetable peels, paper, cotton
Materials that cannot be broken down by decomposers; persist in environment; e.g., plastics, metals, DDT; cause pollution
First animal in food chain; eats producers (plants); e.g., grasshopper eating grass; also called herbivore
Animal that eats primary consumers; e.g., frog eating grasshopper; carnivore at second consumer level
Animal that eats secondary consumers; top predator in most food chains; e.g., eagle eating snake; most affected by biomagnification
Self-feeding organisms that produce their own food from inorganic substances using light (photosynthesis) or chemical energy
Organisms that cannot make their own food; must consume other organisms; includes all animals, fungi and most bacteria
